title: A Systematic, Taxonomy-Guided Survey of Predictive Maintenance in Robotic Systems: Fault Detection, Diagnosis, Prognosis, and Fault-Tolerant Control
content: Robotic systems have become critical assets across manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, and field operations, yet their maintenance remains fragmented across a literature that treats sensing, actuation, mechanical wear, and system-level failure as unrelated topics rather than facets of a single problem. This survey addresses that fragmentation by organizing robot fault detection, diagnosis, prognosis, and fault-tolerant control around a unified four-category taxonomy, sensor, actuator, mechanical, and system-level faults, applied consistently across eight robot platforms: industrial robotic arms, wheeled mobile robots, legged robots, collaborative robots, aerial robots, surgical robots, underwater robots, and humanoid robots. Following a PRISMA-inspired screening process across four databases (IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, Scopus, and ScienceDirect) covering publications from 2022 to 2026, an initial pool of approximately 1,800 identified records was narrowed through duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment to 115 studies meeting this survey's inclusion criteria. Within this literature, industrial robotic arms account for the largest share of coverage, while acoustic emission sensing, optical and fiber Bragg grating sensing, communication-layer system faults, and humanoid-specific fault detection are addressed by a comparatively small number of studies despite the same search effort applied uniformly across every category. Methods are reviewed independently of fault category, spanning classical machine learning, deep learning architectures including recurrent, convolutional, state-space, and generative models, graph neural networks, federated learning, hybrid approaches, and model-based probabilistic methods. Recurring challenges are identified across the reviewed literature, including data scarcity relative to normal operating hours, heterogeneous data across robot fleets, domain shift between laboratory and deployment conditions, sensor corruption under real-world noise, real-time feasibility on constrained onboard hardware, and platform-specific limitations most pronounced for humanoid, surgical, and underwater robots. This survey does not propose new fault-detection algorithms; its contribution is the taxonomy itself and the structured synthesis of existing methods against it, together with a research agenda mapping identified challenges to near-term, mid-term, and long-term directions for the field.
